c1-77.title: Life on the frontier
c1-77.story: On Saturday, Anna and Max visited a small museum about life on the American [[frontier]]. The first room told the story of a [[pioneer]] family who crossed the plains in a wooden wagon. Next to it, a map showed where each [[colonist]] had settled along the river. Max was fascinated by a fur coat that once belonged to a [[trapper]] who spent whole winters alone in the woods. In the next hall, the museum had rebuilt an old [[saloon]], complete with a piano and swinging doors. A guide explained that news from the East used to arrive by [[telegraph]], often days after the events. Anna's favorite display was a poster for a traveling [[charlatan]] who promised to cure everything from headaches to heartbreak. He sold a bright green [[elixir]] that, according to the label, was mostly sugar and alcohol. "Real help came from the local [[healer]], who knew which plants actually worked," the guide added. On the way home, Max joked that his grandmother's herbal tea was the only miracle cure he trusted.

c1-78.title: Dark times in history
c1-78.story: Anna's grandfather came to her university to give a talk about the darkest chapters of the twentieth century. He began by explaining how [[fascism]] grew out of fear, poverty, and anger after the First World War. In Germany, the [[national socialists|national socialist]] used propaganda and violence to crush any opposition. He showed a photo of an ancient Indian temple to point out that the [[swastika]] had been a peaceful symbol for thousands of years before it was stolen. Then his voice grew quieter as he spoke about the [[genocide]] of the Holocaust and the millions of lives it took. A student asked whether these regimes were the only danger, and he replied that [[imperialism]] had also caused enormous suffering across the world. He added that in some countries, a military [[junta]] later seized power and silenced journalists for years. At the end, he told the students that remembering history is the best way to protect democracy. Anna felt proud of him as the room filled with applause.

c1-79.title: Church and faith
c1-79.story: Ira invited Anna to a lecture on the history of Christianity at the city library. The speaker began with the Middle Ages, when a powerful [[inquisitor]] could put anyone on trial for their beliefs. She showed a portrait of a [[cardinal]] in scarlet robes, painted in Rome in the sixteenth century. Then she described daily life in a monastery, where the [[abbot]] made every important decision. Serious disagreements were settled at a [[synod]], where church leaders sometimes argued for weeks. Ira, who was raised a [[Protestant]], asked how the Reformation changed the relationship with [[Catholicism]]. The speaker explained that the reformers kept only two of the seven rituals, and that baptism remained a [[sacrament]] for almost everyone. She also mentioned later movements, such as the [[Baptist]] churches in England and the [[Mormon]] community that eventually settled in Utah. Afterward, Anna noticed a small wooden [[crucifix]] above the library door and wondered how long it had hung there. Ira laughed and said it had probably outlived several librarians.

c1-80.title: Faiths of the world
c1-80.story: For her world religions course, Anna had to interview people of different faiths. First, she visited a mosque in Kyiv, where a friendly [[imam]] explained how Friday prayers are organized. He mentioned that in some countries a religious teacher is called a [[mullah]], and that the word [[cleric]] covers many different roles. When Anna asked about the news, he said calmly that an [[Islamist]] political movement does not speak for most Muslims. The next weekend, Anna and Lisa went on a meditation [[retreat]] in the Carpathian Mountains. Their teacher had studied for years with a Tibetan [[lama]] and spoke softly about letting go of desire. According to Buddhism, he said, this path eventually leads to [[nirvana]]. Lisa was more interested in the yoga class, where the instructor talked about balancing each [[chakra]] and the idea of [[yin]] and yang. By Sunday evening, Anna had a notebook full of interviews and a new [[mantra]]: "One deadline at a time."

c1-81.title: Myths and magic
c1-81.story: Sofia threw a costume party with one rule: everyone had to dress as a creature or figure from world folklore. Max arrived as a [[ghoul]], with gray face paint and a torn jacket that frightened the neighbor's cat. Lisa chose a cheerful Irish [[leprechaun]], complete with a green hat and a pot of chocolate coins. Ira went for something darker and played a [[banshee]], wailing dramatically every time someone opened the door. Anna came as a [[jinn]] from the Arabian Nights, wrapped in blue silk and carrying a brass lamp. Taras wore a long white robe and a fake beard, insisting he was a Celtic [[druid]] and not a wizard. Sofia herself dressed as a Siberian [[shaman]] with a painted drum. Later, someone asked about [[voodoo]], and Ira explained that it is a real religion, not just a horror-movie cliché. The prize for best costume went to Taras, who had also carved a tiny [[totem]] out of a carrot. He wore a cardboard [[amulet]] around his neck and claimed it gave him a winning [[aura]].

c1-82.title: The end of the world
c1-82.story: On Friday night, Anna and Max went to a film club that was showing an old thriller about the end of the world. In the story, a quiet village believes a young stranger is the [[messiah]], until strange things begin to happen. Soon the local priest becomes convinced that the boy is actually the [[antichrist]]. In one striking scene, a stained-glass window of an [[archangel]] shatters during a storm. By the final act, the whole town is preparing for [[armageddon]]. During the discussion afterward, an older man argued that the film criticized blind [[dogma]] rather than religion itself. A student replied that it seemed closer to [[atheism]], since no miracle ever saves the characters. Max said the ending, with its empty church and ringing bells, was a complete [[enigma]] to him. Anna smiled and suggested they watch a comedy next week.
